system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 16 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and peripheral vascular disease, was admitted with worsening dyspnea on exertion, chest pressure, and significant lower extremity and abdominal swelling. He had recently been discharged after treatment for volume overload and DVT. Evaluation revealed acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with volume overload, confirmed by elevated BNP, chest imaging, and physical findings. He was treated with IV furosemide, transitioned to oral torsemide 60 mg daily, and had his tacrolimus increased to maintain therapeutic levels. A cardiac catheterization showed chronic total occlusion of the RCA and mild LAD disease, not requiring intervention. Carotid ultrasound revealed complete occlusion of the right internal carotid artery and 60-69% stenosis on the left, with outpatient vascular follow-up planned. His INR was subtherapeutic on admission, requiring heparin bridging until warfarin achieved therapeutic effect. He was also started on potassium supplementation for hypokalemia. By discharge, his symptoms improved, weight decreased from 92.9 kg to 89.5 kg, and he was stable on adjusted medications with follow-up arranged.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease
Occlusion and stenosis of bilateral carotid arteries
Hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease with heart failure and stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease

previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and peripheral vascular disease, was admitted with worsening dyspnea on exertion, chest pressure, and significant lower extremity and abdominal swelling. He had recently been discharged after treatment for volume overload and DVT. Evaluation revealed acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with volume overload, confirmed by elevated BNP, chest imaging, and physical findings. He was treated with IV furosemide, transitioned to oral torsemide 60 mg daily, and had his tacrolimus increased to maintain therapeutic levels. A cardiac catheterization showed chronic total occlusion of the RCA and mild LAD disease, not requiring intervention. Carotid ultrasound revealed complete occlusion of the right internal carotid artery and 60-69% stenosis on the left, with outpatient vascular follow-up planned. His INR was subtherapeutic on admission, requiring heparin bridging until warfarin achieved therapeutic effect. He was also started on potassium supplementation for hypokalemia. By discharge, his symptoms improved, weight decreased from 92.9 kg to 89.5 kg, and he was stable on adjusted medications with follow-up arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You were admitted because of shortness of breath. We saw fluid in your lungs on the X-ray, and your labs show your kidneys aren’t filtering as well as they should right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling more winded, even just walking to the bathroom. And I’ve been nauseated since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with fluid overload. Your heart isn’t pumping efficiently, which causes fluid to back up into your lungs and affects your kidneys. We’re starting IV furosemide to help you pass more urine and reduce that fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was just in the hospital a few weeks ago for something similar. I’m tired of this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This time, we’re looking closely at why it’s happening again. Your BNP is very high, which confirms heart failure. But we also noticed your creatinine jumped to 3.5, so we’re watching your transplant kidney function carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray shows some improvement in the lung fluid, but we’re concerned because you’re needing more oxygen now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit more breathless this morning. Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The CT scan shows pneumonia in the left side of your lungs. That could be making it harder to breathe. We’re starting antibiotics—cefepime and azithromycin—to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I was on azithromycin before I came in. Why didn’t it help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes pneumonia in patients on immunosuppressants like tacrolimus can be harder to treat. We’re using a stronger antibiotic now and will narrow it later if we find the exact cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count went up, which suggests the infection is still active. We’re switching from vancomycin to just cefepime since the MRSA screen was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the infection spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. The rise in white cells means your body is fighting, but the antibiotics are helping. We’ll keep monitoring your oxygen and repeat the X-ray soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re not making much urine, and your potassium is high. We’re moving you to the ICU for closer monitoring and starting a continuous furosemide drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not peeing at all? Is my kidney failing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s acute kidney injury on top of your chronic stage 4 disease. The transplant team reviewed your ultrasound—no rejection signs. This is likely from poor heart-kidney interaction, called cardiorenal syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You seemed confused last night. We did a head CT—it shows no stroke or bleed. Your confusion was likely from high blood sugar and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much from last night. Was I having a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the scan was clear. We think it was metabolic encephalopathy—your body was under stress from fluid, infection, and high glucose. You’re much more alert now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My blood sugar has always been hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, endocrinology adjusted your insulin. You’re now on 52 units of Lantus in the morning and Humalog with meals. That should help stabilize your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine peaked at 5.4 but is now down to 4.1. You’re making more urine, which is a great sign. We’re weaning the IV diuretic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my kidney is recovering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. As your heart failure improves, your kidney function is following. We’ll keep you on close watch, but this is a positive trend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low when you came in, so we bridged with heparin. Now that your warfarin dose is adjusted, your clotting is in range. You’ll go home on 2.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin since my DVT. Is it still necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of your atrial fibrillation and history of DVT. Your CHADS-VASc score is high, so lifelong anticoagulation reduces stroke risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CO2 angiogram to check your renal arteries. Good news—it showed no significant blockages. So your kidney issues aren’t from new stenosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about another stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No stent needed. Your transplant artery has high resistive indices, but they’re unchanged from before, so it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pneumonia is responding. We’re down to five days of antibiotics and will finish the course tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less short of breath. Is that from the antibiotics or the diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both. The diuretics cleared the fluid, and the antibiotics are treating the infection. Your latest X-ray shows improvement in both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart echo shows preserved ejection fraction—your heart muscle is strong, but it’s stiff and doesn’t relax well. That’s why fluid builds up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not weak, just stiff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, or HFpEF. We’re increasing your carvedilol to 37.5 mg twice daily to help control your heart rate and reduce strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your labs show creatinine down to 1.9, potassium normal, and your chest X-ray is much clearer. We’re moving you back to the floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We’ll switch you to oral torsemide 100 mg daily and make sure you stay stable on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tacrolimus level was 7.5 on admission, now it’s 5.7. We’re keeping it at 4 mg twice daily. The level is therapeutic, so your transplant is protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always worried about rejection. Is that still a risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team is not concerned. No signs of rejection on ultrasound or labs. Your kidney is stable despite the acute injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your weight is down, breathing is better, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home to stay out of the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds, especially the torsemide and warfarin. Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than 3 pounds in a day, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your heart failure team or go to the ER. Also watch for swelling, fever, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have so many pills. Can we simplify them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve streamlined them. You’re off amlodipine for now. Your blood pressure is well-controlled with other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge labs look good: creatinine 2.2, potassium 3.8, and no signs of infection. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What follow-ups do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary care doctor in a week, nephrology and cardiology in two weeks. You’ll need INR and kidney labs monitored regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my PSA was 6.7—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly elevated. Your urologist will recheck it in a few months. No need for alarm now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the faint spots on my brain scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are old, likely from small vessel disease. Your neurologist suggests a cognitive screen later to check for any subtle changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been forgetful lately. Maybe that’s why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll get you referred. For now, focus on rest, meds, and follow-up. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Breathing easier, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your exam shows clear lungs, no edema, and stable vitals. You’re cleared to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Call us with any concerns. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m calling to check in. How’s your breathing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, Doctor. I’ve been weighing myself—no sudden gains.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep it up. See you in clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for calling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your discharge summary is ready. You were admitted for heart failure and pneumonia, and you responded well to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like a new man. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. Just keep following the plan, and we’ll keep you stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and peripheral vascular disease, was admitted with shortness of breath due to acute on chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and pulmonary edema. He developed acute kidney injury likely from cardiorenal syndrome and was found to have concomitant pneumonia, which was treated with antibiotics. He became anuric and was managed in the ICU with aggressive diuresis, including a furosemide drip, which restored urine output and improved renal function. His mental status declined temporarily due to metabolic encephalopathy, but resolved without acute neurological injury. His INR was subtherapeutic, requiring heparin bridging before warfarin stabilization. A CO2 angiogram showed no renal artery stenosis. By discharge, he was breathing comfortably, his labs had normalized, and he was transitioned to oral torsemide 100 mg daily, increased carvedilol, and adjusted insulin. He was discharged home with services, with follow-up planned and instructions to monitor weight and symptoms.
